desc:
A directed graph has n = graph.length nodes labelled 0 to n - 1. The list graph[i] holds the nodes that node i points to. A node without outgoing edges is terminal.

A token is placed on a node and then moved along outgoing edges, one edge per move, choosing any edge it likes, until it stands on a terminal node, where it must stop. A node is k-safe if, whatever choices are made, the token is guaranteed to stop after at most k moves. A terminal node needs 0 moves, so it is k-safe for every k ≥ 0; a node from which the token can wander forever is never k-safe.

Return all k-safe nodes in increasing order.

graph = [[1,2],[2],[3],[]], k = 2  ->  [1,2,3]
(longest walks: from 0 it is 3 moves, from 1 it is 2, from 2 it is 1, node 3 is terminal)

graph = [[1],[0],[]], k = 5        ->  [2]
constraints: The total number of edges is at most 6,000
graph[i] holds distinct values in [0, n - 1]; it may contain i itself
hints: For every node you want the number of moves in the worst case. What is that for a terminal node, and how does it follow from the targets of a non-terminal node?
The worst-case number of moves of a node is 1 plus the largest worst case among its targets. It is infinite if the node can reach a cycle.

Reverse the edges and run Kahn's algorithm from the terminal nodes (out-degree counters). When you finish a node j, update each predecessor i with depth[i] = max(depth[i], depth[j] + 1). Nodes that never get their counter to zero can loop forever. Report the finished nodes with depth at most k.
editorial: Let depth(v) be the largest number of moves the token can make from v before stopping. For a terminal node it is 0, and otherwise it is 1 + max(depth(w)) over all targets w, provided every target has a finite depth. If some target can reach a cycle, the token can circle forever and the node is never safe. The answer is the set of nodes with a finite depth that is at most k.

Compute depths with a reversed Kahn's algorithm. Keep remaining[i], the number of targets of i whose depth is not final yet, starting at the out-degree. Push the terminal nodes. When a node j is popped its depth is final; for every predecessor i set depth[i] = max(depth[i], depth[j] + 1) and decrease remaining[i]; at zero, i's depth is final and it joins the stack. Nodes on a cycle, or with a path into a cycle, keep a positive counter forever and are never reported.

Finally collect the nodes with counter zero and depth at most k, in increasing order. The cost is O(n + m) plus the final sort (which you can avoid by scanning the nodes in order). This is the 'safe states' idea from cycle detection with an extra bound on the longest path.
